title: What are payback and NPV, and how do they decide investment cases?
description: Why money today is worth more than money tomorrow, and how payback, discounting and NPV help decide whether an investment is worth it.
hook: Investment cases often mention payback, NPV or discount rates, and these terms can make people nervous. The idea underneath them is something you already know: £100 today is worth more than £100 in five years. Once that clicks, the rest follows.
body:
Why money today is worth more

Money you have today can be invested and grow. And money promised in the future is uncertain. So when a company spends money now to earn money later, it needs to be paid back more than it spent, to make up for the wait and the risk.

Payback: the simple version

Payback asks how long it takes to earn back the investment. A machine costing £2 million that saves £500,000 a year pays back in 4 years. It is easy and very common in cases. Its weakness: it ignores what happens after payback, and it treats a pound in year four the same as a pound today. Compare it with the asset's life: a 4-year payback on a machine that lasts 3 years is a bad deal.

Discounting

To compare money at different times, we shrink future money back to today's value. At a 10% discount rate, £110 next year is worth £100 today. The discount rate reflects the return investors could get elsewhere at similar risk, often called the cost of capital.

NPV

Net present value adds up all the future cash flows, each shrunk back to today, and subtracts the upfront cost. If NPV is positive, the investment earns more than the cost of capital, so it creates value. In a case you will rarely calculate a full NPV, but you should know what it means and when to mention it.

A useful shortcut: perpetuities

If something pays the same amount every year forever, its value today is roughly the yearly amount divided by the discount rate. £1 million a year at 10% is worth about £10 million. This is handy for quick valuations.

How to talk about it

The project pays back in about four years, which is within the client's five-year target. Since the equipment lasts around ten years, it should create value well beyond payback.

Why the timing of cash flows changes the recommendation

Two projects each promise £1.2 million in total cash receipts. Project A pays £400,000 in each of the next three years. Project B pays nothing for two years and £1.2 million in year three. At a 10% discount rate, A's receipts are worth about £995,000 today, while B's are worth about £902,000. The totals are equal, but the earlier cash flows have more value.

This is also why simple payback and net present value answer different questions. Payback tells you how long it takes to recover the initial investment on an undiscounted basis. NPV discounts every future incremental cash flow and subtracts the upfront commitment. A positive NPV creates value under the chosen assumptions and discount rate; it does not guarantee the forecast will happen.

During a case, check whether cash flows are before or after tax, whether the initial investment includes working capital, and whether the final year includes residual value. You do not have to calculate a complex model aloud. A clean timeline of cash inflows and outflows will often surface the most important issue.
